Orchot Tzadikim 7:13: And you should discern and understand the greatness of this trait, that the Creator conducts Himself by it with all His creatures, as it is said (Psalms 145:9), "and His mercies are over all His works."
Orchot Tzadikim 8:2: Cruelty is the opposite of compassion, as it is written, "they are cruel, and will not show mercy" (Jeremiah 50:42). And this trait is not found in the righteous, but is in the soul of the wicked, as it is written (Proverbs 12:10), "but the mercies of the wicked are cruel." And this trait is also found in the brazen-faced, as it is written (Deuteronomy 28:50), "a brazen-faced nation, that will not show favor to the elder, nor be gracious to the young." And you already know the evil of the trait of insolence. Go and learn the evil of cruelty, for regarding the recompense due a bad man, the rebel and the defiant one, it is said (Proverbs 17:11), "a rebel only seeks evil, and a cruel messenger shall be sent against him." No cruel person practices acts of kindness, as it is written (Proverbs 11:17), "the kind man does good to his own soul, but the cruel man troubles his own flesh."
Orchot Tzadikim 8:3: The cruel man is very far from the good traits, for he will not show compassion to the poor, will not lend to them in their time of need, and will give them nothing. And it is written (Proverbs 19:17), "he who is gracious to the poor lends to the Lord"; and it is said (Psalms 112:5), "good is the man who is gracious and lends, who conducts his affairs with justice"; and it says (ibid. 41:2), "happy is he who considers the poor; the Lord will deliver him in the day of evil" — and all these are the opposite of the cruel man.
Orchot Tzadikim 8:4: He also does not grieve over the troubles of his fellows, as you see with David the king, who said (Psalms 35:13), "but as for me, when they were sick, my clothing was sackcloth, I afflicted my soul with fasting, and my prayer returned into my own bosom." And of Job it is written (Job 30:25), "did I not weep for him whose day was hard, was not my soul grieved for the needy?" — and all this is far from the cruel man. And this trait is found only in men whose nature is like the nature of lions, who tear and rob. And when the wrathful soul grows powerful within a person, the trait of compassion flees, and cruelty grows strong to destroy and to tear down, as it is written (Proverbs 27:4), "cruelty is [in] wrath, and a flood is [in] anger" — there is no wrath like the wrath of cruelty. But in the attribute of the Blessed Creator you find, "in wrath remember mercy" (Habakkuk 3:2); but it is far from a person to show mercy at a time of anger. And there is a further trait in a person's soul: to seek revenge on his enemies, as it is written (Proverbs 6:34), "and he will show no pity on the day of vengeance." Its meaning: when there is vengeance, there is no pity, but only cruelty. And the verse says (Leviticus 19:18), "you shall not take vengeance nor bear a grudge" — we were warned even against bearing a grudge in the heart, how much more so against actually striking one's fellow with the hands. Behold, one should not rejoice even if his enemy falls without his own wrongdoing, as it is written (Proverbs 24:17), "do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles." And whoever takes vengeance and bears a grudge does not overlook the wrongs done to him, and does not forgive his fellows who have wronged him, and this brings about strife and hatred. And you already know how good and how pleasant is the trait of peace.
Orchot Tzadikim 8:5: And included in cruelty is one who robs his fellow of anything belonging to him, and thereby causes him grief. And there is a great punishment for robbing a poor man, and one is liable for death for it, as it is written (Proverbs 22:22), "do not rob the poor, because he is poor"; and it is written (ibid. verse 23), "for the Lord will plead their cause, and rob the life of those who rob them." And even though there are great and grave transgressions worse than robbery, the punishment for robbery is very severe, as it is written of the generation of the Flood (Genesis 6:13), "the end of all flesh has come before Me, for the earth is filled with violence through them." Our Sages said (Sanhedrin 108a): a basket full of sins — none prosecutes as harshly among them all as robbery. And whoever causes grief to an orphan and a widow by robbery, or by humiliation or any kind of grief, is liable for death at the hand of Heaven. And likewise the judges, who have the power to save them from the hand of their oppressors and do not judge the case of the orphan and the widow fairly — they are deserving of death, as it is written (Exodus 22:21), "you shall not afflict any widow or orphan"; and it is written (ibid. verse 22), "if you afflict him at all, and he cries at all to Me, I will surely hear his cry"; and it is written (ibid. verse 23), "and My wrath shall grow hot, and I will kill you with the sword, and your wives shall be widows, and your children fatherless." Measure for measure: your wives shall be widows, corresponding to the affliction of widows; your children fatherless, corresponding to the affliction of orphans.
Orchot Tzadikim 8:6: And whoever causes grief to any person of Israel transgresses a negative commandment, as it is said (Leviticus 25:17), "and you shall not wrong one another" — and this "you shall not wrong" refers to wronging with words (Bava Metzia 58b). Our Sages of blessed memory said (ibid. 59a): all the gates [of prayer] are locked, except the gates of wronging [through words]. Therefore let every person be careful not to cause his fellow grief in any way, neither in deed nor in words.
Orchot Tzadikim 8:7: Whoever robs a poor man is as though he took his very life; and even if he robbed him of a small thing, such as a single coin, he is liable for death (Bava Kamma 119a). This too is part of the trait of cruelty: giving a bad name to one's fellow, thereby causing grief and shame. And whoever gives a bad name that impugns a family's lineage has no atonement, ever.
Orchot Tzadikim 8:8: "You shall not be to him as a creditor" (Exodus 22:24) — meaning that one should not cause grief to the borrower, and the lender should not pass before him when he knows the borrower has nothing with which to repay, for he thereby oppresses him (Bava Metzia 75b). And we were warned to remove the trait of cruelty from our souls, as it is written (Exodus 22:21), "you shall not afflict any widow or orphan"; and it is said (Leviticus 25:17), "and you shall not wrong one another, but you shall fear your God." Also, to return the pledge to a poor man, as it is written (Exodus 22:25), "if you take your neighbor's garment as a pledge, you shall return it to him before the sun goes down"; and it is said (ibid. verse 26), "and it shall be that when he cries to Me, I will hear, for I am gracious"; and it is said (ibid. verse 20), "you shall not wrong a stranger, nor oppress him."
Orchot Tzadikim 8:9: He should also keep cruelty far even from an animal, as it is written (Proverbs 12:10), "a righteous man knows the soul of his animal" — not to burden it excessively, and not to starve it. And so it is written (Exodus 23:5), "if you see the donkey of your enemy lying under its burden, and would refrain from helping him, you shall surely help him." And our Sages said (Bava Metzia 32b): the pain of living creatures is a Torah-level matter. And if you are a man who is feared, whose awe is cast upon others, so that whatever you command them they are afraid to refuse — be very careful not to burden them heavily, even to heat a jug of water, or to go out on an errand to the marketplace of the city merely to buy a loaf of bread. And of this it is said in the Torah (Leviticus 25:46), "but over your brothers, the children of Israel, one over another, you shall not rule with rigor." And by this we were warned that a person should not make his fellow do hard labor, and should command him only to do what he does willingly and with his own consent. And with a Canaanite slave, it is permitted to work him with rigor; nonetheless it is a trait of piety to be merciful, and not burden him with a heavy yoke, and not to disgrace him, neither by hand nor by word: the verse handed him over for labor, not for disgrace (Niddah 47a). And one should speak to him gently even in a time of dispute, and listen to his claims. And so Job said (Job 31:13-15), "if I have despised the cause of my manservant or my maidservant when they had a grievance against me — what then shall I do when God rises up, and when He visits, what shall I answer Him? Did not He who made me in the womb make him? And did not the same One form us both in the womb?"
Orchot Tzadikim 8:10: The early sages would give their servants a portion of every single dish they themselves ate, and would feed their animals and their servants before sitting down to their own meal (Berachot 40a), for indeed it says (Psalms 123:2), "behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master, as the eyes of a maidservant to the hand of her mistress, so our eyes look to the Lord our God, until He is gracious to us." And the pious man gave his servant first, from every single dish, before he himself ate, and by the merit of this Elijah made a point of speaking with him (Ketubot 61a).
Orchot Tzadikim 8:11: The Torah said (Leviticus 19:18), "and you shall love your fellow as yourself" — and whoever has the trait of cruelty is very far from this. Other people are never at ease with the cruel man, and he finds no favor in the eyes of the world.
Orchot Tzadikim 8:12: And even in a place of rebuke we were warned not to rebuke one's fellow with cruelty, as it is written (ibid. verse 17), "you shall surely rebuke your fellow, and not bear sin because of him."
Orchot Tzadikim 8:13: Its meaning: do not rebuke him harshly and with cruelty so as to shame him, or you will bear sin because of him. Until now we have related the evil of cruelty. But there are places where one must act with cruelty against the wicked, in the manner Job spoke (Job 29:17), "and I broke the jaws of the unjust, and plucked the prey out of his teeth"; and as the Torah said, to put the wicked to death and to flog them. And so our Sages said (Ketubot 86a): whoever does not wish to make a sukkah, or tzitzit for his garment, or a mezuzah for his doorway, is beaten until his life departs. All this requires cruelty — to pursue the wicked and press hard upon them, to bring them back to the good.
Orchot Tzadikim 8:14: And one must be cruel in judgment, showing no mercy to his relatives and loved ones and to the poor, but must render judgment upon them [strictly according to the law]. And our Sages further said (Eruvin 22a): in whom do you find the words of Torah? In one who makes himself cruel toward his children, like a raven. Such as Rav Adda bar Matna, who was going to the study hall, and his wife said to him: what shall I do with your children? And he answered her: are there not vegetable stalks in the marsh?
Orchot Tzadikim 8:15: For this is a clear matter: whoever shows too much compassion to his children, through this thinks only of earning money, and gives no thought to whether the money comes to him permissibly or forbiddenly, for love corrupts the proper order. And also, out of the toil he undertakes day and night to provide their food and needs in abundance, he becomes idle from the words of Torah, for he makes his business affairs his main concern; and through this all his deeds become disordered.
Orchot Tzadikim 8:16: And one must be cruel toward the wicked, showing them no mercy. And our Sages said (Kohelet Rabbah 7:33): whoever makes himself merciful in a place [that calls for] cruelty will end up making himself cruel in a place [that calls for] mercy. And so you find with King Saul: because he showed mercy to Agag, Haman came forth from him, who became an oppressor of Israel (Megillah 13a). One should also be cruel toward his own body, constantly toiling to do the will of the Blessed Creator, and not show his body mercy by indulging it and letting it follow the wantonness of its heart; rather, he should be cruel toward himself, to subdue his evil inclination, to live a life of hardship and to occupy himself with Torah and fulfill the commandments, even if this is very hard for him. But he should not be excessively cruel toward himself so as to ruin his body; rather, he should take hold of a middle measure.
Orchot Tzadikim 8:17: And you, O son of man, examine yourself and distance yourself from cruelty; but show compassion to the poor and needy, and let the poor become members of your household: "and He will show you mercy, and have compassion upon you" (Deuteronomy 13:18) — whoever shows compassion to his fellow creatures is shown compassion from Heaven (Shabbat 151b). Therefore do not remove compassion from yourself, but keep guard against the trait of cruelty; and Solomon said, "lest you give your glory to others, and your years to a cruel one" (Proverbs 5:9). And be careful of the vengeance that stems from cruelty. Rather, if you wish to take revenge on your enemies, add good qualities to yourself and walk in upright ways, and by this you will take revenge on your enemy, for he will be pained at your good qualities and your good name, and will mourn upon hearing your good reputation. But if you do disgraceful deeds, your enemy will rejoice at your disgrace and your shame, and behold, he thereby takes revenge on you.
Orchot Tzadikim 8:18: And if you wish to show compassion to your children and your relatives and to bring them great honor, occupy yourself with Torah and good deeds and acts of kindness. This is very good for them, that they be honored through you and not bear disgrace because of you. There is no greater shame than for one whose fathers and relatives are wicked, such as one whose father was a thief and a robber, or committed other well-known deeds disgraceful in the eyes of the world — all his offspring are disgraced after him for generation upon generation, for people will say: these are the offspring of that wicked man! Also, because of the iniquity of fathers, sons die, as it is written (Exodus 20:5), "visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, to the third and fourth generation." See and understand: is there anyone more cruel than one whose children die because of his sin?! And there is no one who shows more compassion to his children than the righteous man, for his merit stands for a thousand generations.
Orchot Tzadikim 8:19: Abraham bound his son, and the Holy One, blessed be He, swore to remember that merit for his children throughout all generations. And at the time Israel sinned with the [Golden] Calf, Moses our teacher, peace upon him, stood in prayer and said (Exodus 32:13), "remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, Your servants." And likewise Solomon (2 Chronicles 6:42), "remember the mercies of David Your servant" — and they were answered. And so we mention the merit of the Fathers every day.
Orchot Tzadikim 8:20: Therefore know that there are none more cruel than those who commit transgressions. For because of the sin of baseless hatred the Second Temple was destroyed (Yoma 9b). And all calamities that come upon the world come because of transgressions, as our Sages, peace upon them, said (Shabbat 32b): because of the sin of [neglecting] challah, there is no blessing in what is gathered in; because of the sin of neglecting terumah and tithes, the heavens are held back; because of the sin of delaying judgment, and perverting judgment, and corrupting judgment, and the sin of neglecting Torah study — the sword and great plunder, pestilence and famine come upon the world. And so with many other things. And in truth, those who cause these calamities are cruel toward themselves, toward their children, and toward the people of their generation, while the righteous are merciful toward them, toward their children, and toward their generation — as we say (Berachot 17b), that the entire world is sustained by the merit of Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa.
Orchot Tzadikim 8:21: This is also an answer to the poor who say: with what shall we do good? We have nothing in hand to give as charity to the poor. But these are vain words, for one can give charity through his good deeds and through fulfilling the commandments, being careful in the service of the Blessed Creator with all his ability; and by the merit of the good and the righteous, the Holy One, blessed be He, does good to the world and sustains it. Is there any charity greater than this?! Also, let the poor man give a little charity, even if he himself is sustained by charity, and his reward will be doubled and redoubled, for the little he gives is accounted like the great gift of the rich man. And so our Sages said (Menachot 110a): whether one gives much or little, so long as he directs his heart to his Father in Heaven.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:2: Joy. This trait comes to a person because of great ease in his heart, without any harmful mishap. And a person who attains his desires, and to whom nothing happens that grieves him, will have constant joy. And whoever has constant joy — his face shines, his complexion glows, his body is healthy, and old age does not hasten upon him, as it is said (Proverbs 17:22), "a joyful heart makes for good healing." And from joy comes laughter to a person. But it is not fitting for an intelligent man to indulge much in laughter, for a light-headedness accompanies laughter, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 7:6), "for like the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool." And it has already been said that it is a sign of a fool to laugh in a place where laughter is not fitting. And it is not fitting for one who has ethical discipline to conduct himself with laughter in assemblies and gatherings, because it is said: whoever laughs a great deal diminishes his own fear of Heaven, for at the time of laughter one cannot direct his mind to any fear of the Lord God. How much more so if he indulges in games of chance or dice, where the fear of God is not upon him at all. Therefore a person should discipline himself not to laugh, and not to take for himself a teacher or a companion who indulges in laughter, as it is said (Jeremiah 15:17), "I did not sit in the assembly of merrymakers, nor did I rejoice"; and it is written (Proverbs 14:23), "in all labor there is profit [but the talk of the lips leads only to poverty]."
Orchot Tzadikim 9:3: There are many evils in joy and laughter. Such as one who rejoices at his fellow's misfortune, when some harmful mishap of the world befalls him. Of this it is said (Proverbs 24:17), "do not rejoice when your enemy falls." And there is a joy worse than this: such as rejoicing when his fellow stumbles in the service of the Blessed Creator, or rejoicing at his lack of knowledge. You must understand: a servant who serves the king faithfully ought to grieve upon seeing men rebel against his master and reproach him, and is obligated to rebuke them to their faces and make known their vileness. But if the servant rejoices upon seeing his master's disgrace and shame — this is not a faithful servant, but a companion to a destructive man, and shall bear his iniquity. And behold, the verse says (Psalms 147:11), "the Lord favors those who fear Him," and whoever rejoices at his fellow's stumbling — his will is not like the will of the Blessed Creator. Therefore Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah prayed (Berachot 28b): may my colleagues not stumble in a matter of halachah so that I rejoice over them, and may I not stumble so that they rejoice over me. And Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah prayed this because he saw that this is a common thing — that one rejoices at his fellow's error, so that he may triumph over his fellow and gain a reputation for himself. And even several important people are not careful about this. Therefore, every man whose will is the will of God should grieve that the will of the Lord is not being done. And a person should pray even for his enemy, that he serve the Blessed Creator. And he should direct his intent, in the prayer's blessing of "You are Gracious," and in the blessing of "Return us," and in the blessing of "Forgive us," toward all of Israel — those who love him and those who hate him — and likewise in all the blessings. For how is it possible to pray "Healer of the sick" and the other blessings, when he does not wish that his fellow be healed or gain understanding?!
Orchot Tzadikim 9:4: And because this inclination is very common in the hearts of people, and they do not notice this matter, we have written this to warn those who fear the Lord to prepare their hearts to God with complete and genuine intent, to pour out their souls before the Lord for all of Israel, those who love Him and those who hate Him. And by this one fulfills "and you shall love your fellow as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18). "And the pure of hands shall grow stronger and stronger" (Job 17:9).
Orchot Tzadikim 9:5: There is yet another joy and laughter that is very bad: such as one who mocks whoever is careful in the service of the Blessed Lord and fulfills His commandments. And there are four evils in this:
Orchot Tzadikim 9:6: The first, that he darkens his own soul from the light of the commandments; when he despises and mocks those who fulfill the commandments, the commandments become disgraceful in his own eyes.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:7: The second: that perhaps, because of the mockery, the righteous man will be kept from his righteous deeds, for he cannot bear the mockery.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:8: The third: that many people who have not yet tried to walk in the ways of the Blessed Lord will be unable to do teshuvah because of the mockery, and will walk in darkness all their days. And it turns out that this mocker not only withholds from his fellow the abundant good hidden away for the righteous, but brings him down to the depths of Sheol. And behold, this mocker is included in the punishment of "one who causes the many to sin."
Orchot Tzadikim 9:9: The fourth: he is like a bandit who stands at the crossroads and cuts off the feet of those bringing a gift to the king — is this one not the hater and enemy of the king, and is his wickedness not very great?
Orchot Tzadikim 9:10: There is yet another joy, bitter as wormwood: such as those who pursue adultery and robbery and other transgressions, and rejoice when they attain their evil desires. Of these it is said (Proverbs 2:14), "who rejoice to do evil, and delight in the perversities of evil." And their punishment is great, reaching down to the depths of Sheol.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:11: And there is yet another confused kind of joy, which raises smoke over all the commandments and causes the fear of the Blessed Lord to be forgotten from people's hearts: such as those who become drunk and rejoice in the house of feasting, and after this joy comes sorrow, for many corruptions come from feasting. And who is wiser in wisdom than Solomon son of David, who said (Proverbs 23:29-30), "who has woe, who has sorrow, who has strife, who has complaining, who has wounds without cause, who has redness of eyes? Those who tarry long over wine, those who go to seek out mixed wine." The prophet, too, said (Isaiah 5:11), "woe to those who rise early in the morning to pursue strong drink, who tarry late into the evening until wine inflames them"; and he said (ibid. verse 12), "and the harp and the lute, the tambourine and the flute and wine are at their feasts, but they do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider the deeds of His hands"; and it says (ibid. verse 13), "therefore My people are gone into exile for lack of knowledge, and their honorable men are famished, and their multitude dried up with thirst"; and it says (ibid. verse 14), "therefore Sheol has enlarged its desire, and opened its mouth without measure, and their glory and their multitude and their tumult, and he who rejoices among them, shall descend into it"; and it is said (ibid. 28:7), "but these also have erred through wine, and through strong drink have gone astray; the priest and the prophet have erred through strong drink, they are swallowed up by wine, they have gone astray through strong drink, they err in vision, they stumble in judgment." See what corruption comes from wine! And it is written (Proverbs 20:1), "wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise." See what corruptions come from drunkenness, as it is written (Genesis 9:21), "and he drank of the wine and became drunk, and he uncovered himself within his tent..." — and from this the Canaanites came into the world.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:12: Behold, wine causes one to become a mocker, and to be boisterous and quarrelsome, and whoever is led astray by it gains no wisdom. And Rabbeinu Moshe Maimonides wrote: a gathering for intoxicating drink ought to be, in your eyes, a greater disgrace than a gathering of naked people with their nakedness exposed. And drunkenness is among the causes of evil, for it destroys the intellect that the Blessed Lord breathed into man's nostrils. However, drinking wine is very good when you drink it according to the practice of the intelligent, in the manner Solomon said (Proverbs 31:6-7), "give strong drink to him who is perishing, and wine to those of bitter soul; let him drink and forget his poverty, and remember his misery no more." And it is further said of wine (Judges 9:13), "which cheers God and men"; and it is written (Psalms 104:15), "and wine that gladdens the heart of man." The verse also says (Song of Songs 1:2), "for your love is better than wine"; and it is said (ibid. 7:10), "and your palate like the best wine."
Orchot Tzadikim 9:13: From all these we learn the praise of wine, when it is according to the ruling of the wise and drunk in proper measure, so that the intellect overcomes the wine and the wine does not overcome the intellect; and drunk at a set time with friends and companions, with the pious and the righteous, and not with the empty and the idle. For wine adds the wisdom of the profound, and it is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it. And further: wine adds to the wisdom of the intelligent man, and doubles the folly of the fool; it renews the love of a friend, and stirs up the enmity of an enemy; it opens the hand of the generous man, and strengthens the heart of the miser.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:14: And this is the way of wine drinkers: let him make wine a remedy for his worry, and strengthen himself in Torah, to study it with joy — for as long as a person is in a state of grief, he cannot study. And likewise a court in a state of grief cannot properly clarify the law, whether between kosher and unfit, between permitted and forbidden. Grief also nullifies the intention of the heart in prayer.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:15: Also, when a person is in a state of grief, whoever speaks to him or asks him to do a kindness for him — he has no strength to fulfill the request. And it is written (Isaiah 49:8), "in a time of favor I have answered you."
Orchot Tzadikim 9:16: Therefore, along this path let the intelligent man intend his wine drinking, and be careful not to drink so much that he must neglect his work and his affairs. And above all he should guard against drinking so much that he becomes idle from his Torah study and his prayer, or so much that he indulges in excessive laughter and levity. And he should not drink to the point of revealing his own secrets, or the secrets of others. And if you drink according to this measure, wine will not become a stranger [i.e. a source of harm] to you.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:17: Also on the festivals and holidays, of which it is written (Deuteronomy 12:18), "and you shall rejoice before the Lord your God" — one should not indulge himself in wine beyond what is proper, as it is said (ibid. 28:47), "because you did not serve the Lord your God with joy and gladness of heart" — from this you learn that we were not commanded to have a joy through which one forgets the Maker of all. And it is impossible to serve the Blessed Lord out of levity, nor out of laughter, nor out of drunkenness.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:18: Upon the trait of joy depends the positive commandment that one justify all that befalls him, as it is said (Deuteronomy 8:5), "and you shall know in your heart, that as a man disciplines his son, so the Lord your God disciplines you."
